title: The weaver of Benares
hook: Kabir, a weaver of Kashi, sang the Lord's name in the plain speech of the street

segments.voice: Yesterday, fifteen voices: saints of many backgrounds, side by side with the Gurus in one book. Today we sit down beside the first of them, at his loom.

Clack. Shuttle across. Clack. Beater down. Clack. In the old city of Kashi, also called Benares or Varanasi, a man sits at a loom set into the floor, feet on the pedals, hands throwing the shuttle back and forth, all day. Thread in, cloth out. Somewhere in that rhythm, he starts to sing. And the songs he made at work, or so tradition tells it, travel further than any cloth he ever sold. Some of them end up inside the Guru Granth Sahib. His name is Kabir, and today's word is what he did for a living.
screen: `CLACK. SHUTTLE ACROSS.` → `A LOOM IN KASHI.` → `A MAN SINGS AT WORK.`

segments.voice: Julaha. A weaver. It's not a title somebody gave Kabir later; he uses it about himself. In a hymn in Raag Asa, Kabir speaks to a Brahmin and says, in plain words: you are a Brahmin, and I am a weaver of Kashi. Then he asks the man to grasp what he's saying. He doesn't hide the trade. A weaver in that world was a working man, and some looked down on the work. Kabir sets it right there in the hymn, next to his name, like a signature. Tradition says he grew up in a Muslim family of weavers, and the hymns sing of Ram and Hari, of Allah and the One beyond every name. Sikhs honor him as a bhagat, a devotee of the One. Then there's his language. Kabir's hymns in the Granth often sound less like a temple or a court than like a lane in a market: pots, threads, cows, a dog, a mother, a loom. He took the things in front of him and made them carry God. And here's the turn. Yesterday's roll call in Raag Asa said Kabir left his loom for love of the Lord's feet. Yet the loom never leaves his songs. The work becomes the picture. Whatever he sings about the Lord, he often sings it with a weaver's hands: devotion at the level of the shuttle and the thread.
screen: `I AM A WEAVER OF KASHI.` · `THE TRADE, SET BY HIS NAME.` · `THE SPEECH OF THE MARKET LANE.` · `THE LOOM NEVER LEAVES HIS SONGS.` · then, large: `A WEAVER'S SONG.`

segments.voice: Pick one plain task you'll do today anyway, dishes, typing, folding, driving, and in your mind find the rhythm inside it: a plate in, a plate out; a key, a key, a space. Don't add music; just notice the beat that's already there, and let your breath ride on it. If you pray, you can let Waheguru sit on that beat, once with each round.
Julaha. A weaver. Kabir's own word for himself, a weaver of Kashi, set beside his name in the Guru's book.
Your line: a weaver's song. Work can be where the singing starts. Day seven hundred forty-eight, done.

howItsDone: Sikhs sing Kabir's hymns in kirtan alongside the Gurus' hymns, and his signature 'says Kabir' is heard in gurdwaras in raag after raag.
